## **ABSTRACT** 

_Aims._ Understanding the internal structure of H II regions is fundamental for constraining star formation processes in galaxies. We investigated how the filling factor (FF) relates to luminosity, size, electron density, and Hα equivalent width (EW(Hα)) in H II regions. We also explored the association between star-forming regions and the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-to-dust emission, to assess their possible connection to the evolutionary stages of H II regions. 

_Methods._ We investigated the FF in 622 H II regions in NGC 628 by combining 475 regions from SIGNALS and 147 from PHANGSMUSE using a dedicated analysis pipeline. We derived the luminosity, emission line fluxes, radii, electron densities, and FF. We used PHANGS-JWST survey images to study the spatial relation between the FF and PAH-to-dust emission, quantified by the PAH-to-dust ratio _RPAH_ using James Webb Space Telescope/Mid-Infrared Instrument (JWST/MIRI) emission bands at 7.7, 11.3, and 21 µm. _Results._ Higher Log(FF) and high EW(Hα) values are found in luminous regions, whereas more extended regions with lower EW(Hα) display lower Log(FF) values. We show that the H II radius definition significantly affects the LHα − R relation. Low-luminosity compact H II regions appear to reflect a transition from cluster-powered regions to nebulae that are ionized by single massive stars, with the transition occurring around log(LHα) ∼ 37 erg s[−][1] . The PAH-to-dust ratio RPAH correlates with the volumetric Hα luminosity density, LHα/R[3] , with a transitional range centered around log(LHα/R[3] ) ∼ 32 erg s[−][1] , corresponding to log(FF) ≈−4.4. Regions with lower Log(FF) values exhibit higher RPAH values, suggesting less efficient PAH processing in more porous structures.

The typical spatial resolutions of the SIGNALS and the PHANGS-MUSE surveys in NGC 628 do not allow us to resolve substructures such as rings, shells, or cavities within the analyzed H II regions. We selected a total of 622 H II regions from the SIGNALS and the PHANGS-MUSE H II regions survey. After applying a consistent homogenization of the physical parameters and density measurements in the two surveys, we found that the derived FF values showed very good agreement. The statistical consistency between the distributions confirms the equivalence of the SIGNALS and PHANGS-MUSE datasets for this analysis and provides a robust basis for our subsequent results. results.question: Compare the two studies "Not all cores are equal: Phase-space origins of dynamical friction, stalling and buoyancy" and "From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction": based on the excerpts, how do the dynamical-friction phase-space effects identified in the first paper (plateaus and DF-inflections causing stalling or buoyancy, and the capacity of inspiraling perturbers to reshape the DF) bear on the formation and central migration/merging of massive compact objects (over-massive black holes and compact stellar systems) in the LRD formation scenario described in the second paper? Provide a concise synthesis citing supported statements from each paper.
results.reference_answer:
The two papers are complementary: the DF-phase-space effects from "Not all cores are equal" imply mechanisms that can help explain, modulate, or stall the inward migration and central coalescence invoked in the LRD formation scenario in "From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction". Specifically:

- From "Not all cores are equal": core stalling arises when the host DF develops a plateau that halts inspiral, while dynamical buoyancy can push masses outward when the DF has an inflection; moreover, an inspiraling perturber can reshape the DF, erasing plateaus or creating inflections and thereby changing whether friction continues (evidence_id: 1cae81ac2ad0f0b8249af2d9; b39c49573c4cc4625e188a56).

- From the LRD scenario: LRD formation relies on many star clusters migrating and merging into a central compact stellar system and on formation/merging of over-massive black holes; cluster migration and inward coalescence are central steps in producing the compact central object (evidence_id: 772c200ac6ac54fc84a47dfd; 65304e96ebbfc540f97342bc).

Synthesis: if real galactic hosts that produce LRDs have DFs that develop plateaus or inflections, the migration of clusters and embedded BH seeds could be slowed, stalled off-center, or even reversed by the DF-driven dynamics described in the first paper. Conversely, sufficiently massive inspiraling clusters or BHs could modify the host DF during their approach (erasing plateaus or creating negative gradients), enabling further inward migration and merger—this provides a nonlinear, feedback-regulated pathway that can lengthen or accelerate the timescale for central coalescence in the LRD channel. Thus, the phase-space criteria identified in "Not all cores are equal" are directly relevant to whether the cluster-driven formation and central assembly of over-massive BHs and compact stellar systems in the LRD scenario proceed efficiently or get stalled/wander, and predict that migration outcomes depend on the host DF structure as well as the perturber mass (evidence_id: 1cae81ac2ad0f0b8249af2d9; b39c49573c4cc4625e188a56; 772c200ac6ac54fc84a47dfd; 65304e96ebbfc540f97342bc).
results.answer:
The first paper (Not all cores are equal) identifies two distinct distribution-function features that alter dynamical friction: a plateau in the host DF causes inspiral to stall (core stalling), while an inflection (d f / d E > 0) in the DF renders the system unstable to a growing dipole mode that drives outward motion (dynamical buoyancy). [1] [2]

The first paper reports that an inspiraling perturber can dynamically reshape the host DF: more massive perturbers can erase DF plateaus and re-establish negative gradients that re-enable friction, while lighter objects remain trapped at a plateau producing long-lived off-center configurations. [3]

The first paper states astrophysical implications of these DF-driven outcomes, specifically that core stalling provides a natural explanation for displaced nuclear star clusters and off-centered AGN, that globular clusters in dwarf galaxies can remain from not sinking, and that stalling and buoyancy create a bottleneck for SMBH binary inspiral prior to gravitational-wave emission affecting predicted merger rates. [2] [3]

The second paper (From Feedback-Free Star Clusters to Little Red Dots via Compaction) proposes that Little Red Dots form as compact stellar systems hosting over-massive black holes, originating from thousands of star clusters formed at z>8 and subsequent wet compaction events associated with mergers or colliding cold streams. [4]

Taken together, the two papers imply that the DF-driven stalling and buoyancy mechanisms identified in the first paper could materially affect the central migration and merging of the over-massive black holes and compact stellar systems produced in the Little Red Dots scenario, potentially producing off-center retention or stalled coalescence of such massive objects unless the inspiraling object is sufficiently massive to reshape the DF and re-enable friction. [1] [3] [4]

Because the first paper emphasizes that the overall host distribution function (not just the central density slope) governs whether stalling or buoyancy occur and that structurally similar cores can yield different dynamical outcomes, compact systems formed in the Little Red Dots pathway could nonetheless exhibit diverse central-migration behaviors depending on their phase-space DFs. [4] [5]

In the case of double power-law ( _𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾_ ) models, systems with low _𝛾_ (shallow inner slope) and/or high _𝛼_ (sharp transition) naturally develop plateaus and inflections, explaining why apparently “similar” cores yield dissimilar dynamical outcomes. Hence, not all cores are equal. 

The DF framework also clarifies why more massive perturbers can transiently overcome the stalling barrier: their inspiral dynamically reshapes the DF, erasing existing plateaus and re-establishing negative gradients that re-enable friction. Conversely, lighter objects remain trapped at the plateau, producing long-lived off-center configurations. In addition, even if the DF initially does not have a plateau or inflection, the BH inspiral itself can create an inflection, resulting in its stalling. This self-regulated interplay between the perturber and its host distribution reveals dynamical friction as a fundamentally nonlinear, feedback-driven process, not a static background drag. 

Our results bridge the gap between kinetic theory and cosmological structure formation, offering a unified physical picture of friction, stalling, and buoyancy in cored systems. Future work will extend this framework to more realistic, anisotropic, and time-evolving galaxies, enabling quantitative predictions for the demographics of stalled and wandering black holes across cosmic time. The astrophysical implications are far-reaching. In dwarf galaxies and massive ellipticals, core stalling provides a natural explanation for displaced nuclear star clusters and off-centered AGN. It also accounts for globular clusters in dwarf galaxies which would have otherwise sunk to the center. For SMBH binaries, stalling and buoyancy identify a key bottleneck in the inspiral process prior to binary formation and gravitational-wave emission, influencing predicted merger rates for LISA. This underscores the necessity for an in-depth study of core formation via different mechanisms, focusing in particular on their phase-space distributions, and the resulting dynamics in these systems. One of these mechanisms, self-interacting dark matter, is studied in a follow-up paper (van den Bosch & Dattathri 2026).

Our work follows directly from Dattathri et al. We extend this work here to show that an unstable dipole mode results in outward motion of massive objects, i.e. dynamical buoyancy. Since the DF is determined by the overall density profile of the system, not just the inner power-law slope, our overall conclusion is that not all cores are equal. 

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide background on the phase-space structure of systems with double power-law density profiles and briefly describe the kinetic theory of dynamical friction. Section 3 describes the N-body simulations that we use in this work, as well as the methodology used to analyze these simulations. Section 4 describes the results of our N-body simulations with an infalling perturber, where we show that massive perturbers in systems with very similar density profiles can show markedly different stalling behaviors. In Section 5, we demonstrate that our simulation results can be well explained by studying the phase-space distribution function of the system. Section 6 examines the origin of dynamical buoyancy. We put our results in perspective in Section 7 by discussing the underlying dynamics, comparison with other related studies, and the limitations of our model. We discuss the various astrophysical implications of our findings in Section 8 and conclude in Section 9. 

Throughout this paper, we refer to the massive perturber, which we model as a point particle of fixed mass, as a black hole (BH). We emphasize, though, that most of the results will also hold if the massive perturber were any other object (i.e., a satellite galaxy or globular cluster), as long as its tidal stripping is negligible.

retrieved_chunks.text:
## ABSTRACT 

Dynamical friction governs the orbital decay of massive perturbers within galaxies and dark matter halos, yet its standard Chandrasekhar formulation fails in systems with cores of (roughly) constant density, where inspiral can halt or even reverse, phenomena known respectively as core stalling and dynamical buoyancy. Although these effects have been observed in simulations, the conditions under which they arise remain unclear. Using high-resolution N-body simulations and analytic insights from kinetic theory, we systematically explore the physical origin of these effects. We demonstrate that the overall distribution function (DF) of the host, not just its central density gradient, determines the efficiency and direction of dynamical friction. Core stalling arises when the perturber encounters a plateau in the DF, either pre-existing or dynamically created through its own inspiral, while buoyancy emerges in systems whose DFs possess an inflection that drives an unstable dipole mode. We show that double power-law density profiles with rapid outer-to-inner slope transitions naturally produce such DF features, which is why structurally similar cores can yield radically different dynamical outcomes. Our results provide a unified framework linking the phase-space structure of galaxies to the fate of embedded massive objects, with direct implications for off-center AGN, the dynamics of nuclear star clusters, and the stalled coalescence of black holes in dwarf galaxies and massive ellipticals. 

_Keywords:_ Galaxy evolution – Galaxy dynamics – Orbital resonances – N-body simulations

retrieved_chunks.text: Cosmological simulations coupled with photoionization models provide a powerful tool for predicting emission-line ratios across a wide range of redshifts. Hirschmann et al. (2023a,b) utilized IllustrisTNG simulations coupled with a library of emission-line templates including star formation, AGN, and shocks, while Garg et al. (2024) employed SIMBA simulations integrated with `CLOUDY` to account for H ii regions, post-AGB stars, and diffuse ionized gas. While these studies successfully demonstrate that strong-line ratios evolve with redshift, their predictive power is fundamentally limited by their reliance on pre-defined empirical scaling relations, such as fixed gas densities, empirical N/O–O/H relationship curve, assumed log _𝑈_ –log(O/H) correlation, and an assumed equivalence between stellar and gas-phase metallicities. These models often “lock in” local physics, potentially masking the very environmental diversities that define the high-redshift ISM. Consequently, these frameworks are not fully self-consistent, as the resulting line ratios are largely a reflection of the input empirical constraints rather than an emergent property of the simulated galaxy evolution. Despite using high-redshift simulation data, they remain, in essence, variants of local strong-line calibrations that fail to fundamentally address the issue of unique environmental conditions of the early universe.

results.question: Compare the findings of "Open Clusters as Laboratories for Cool Star Evolution: Highlights from the Cool Stars 23 Splinter Session" and "The internal kinematics and chemistry of 20 Milky Way strings" regarding (1) whether small coeval stellar structures show internal chemical homogeneity comparable to classical open clusters, and (2) what implications each paper offers for the origin or evolution of such structures. Provide a concise synthesis supported by specific statements from both papers and indicate whether the two studies present compatible or differing conclusions.
results.reference_answer: (1) Internal chemical homogeneity: Theia/string study (The internal kinematics and chemistry of 20 Milky Way strings) finds that most of the 20 objects are chemically homogeneous: "Fifteen out of 20 objects crowd together in the −0.10 ≤ [Fe/H] ≤ 0.00 dex and 0.04 ≤ σ[Fe/H] ≤ 0.10 dex range... Most of the objects have a chemical homogeneity comparable to OCs" (evidence_id 7a7283dee098acf2575f1742). The Cool Stars 23 splinter session paper emphasizes open clusters as chemically uniform populations used to study Galactic abundance gradients and reports robust abundance measurements (used as a basis for gradients) and agreement with APOGEE for overlapping elements (evidence_id 00c7f505bf16fbdd5f2b60bb). Thus both papers support that small coeval structures (open clusters, and many strings/Theia objects) exhibit chemical homogeneity comparable to classical open clusters (evidence_ids 7a7283dee098acf2575f1742, 00c7f505bf16fbdd5f2b60bb). (2) Implications for origin/evolution: The Theia/strings paper interprets the chemical homogeneity and age similarity with embedded OCs as evidence that strings "may be remnants of evaporated (or still evaporating) open clusters or objects that formed in star formation hubs" and notes a variety of possible origins including dispersing hubs or filaments (evidence_id fea1bf7065e14405d2b93b7f). The Cool Stars 23 paper uses open clusters as benchmarks to map Galactic abundance gradients (including neutron-capture s-process trends) and highlights clusters (and their tails/unbound populations) as tracers of chemical gradients and dynamical evolution (it documents that abundances with significant s-process enrichment show significantly shallower gradient slopes) and stresses the value of clusters for studying spatial abundance variation (evidence_id 00c7f505bf16fbdd5f2b60bb). Synthesis and compatibility: Both studies are compatible: the Cool Stars 23 paper treats open clusters as chemically homogeneous reference populations for Galactic chemical mapping, while the Theia/strings paper finds that many string-like, extended/coherent groups share similarly low abundance dispersions and may be physically connected to open-cluster formation and dissolution. Together they support a picture in which both bound open clusters and some extended coeval strings preserve chemical signatures useful for tracing formation sites and subsequent dynamical evolution (evidence_ids 00c7f505bf16fbdd5f2b60bb, 7a7283dee098acf2575f1742, fea1bf7065e14405d2b93b7f)."},

## **Abstract** 

Open clusters remain among the most powerful laboratories for calibrating how fundamental stellar properties such as rotation, magnetic activity, surface chemistry, and internal structure evolve over a star’s pre-main-sequence to main-sequence and post-main-sequence lifetime. Because cluster members share a common age, galactic environment, and initial composition, they provide empirical anchors upon which age-dating techniques such as gyrochronology, activity-age relations, and chemical clocks are built. This paper summarizes the Cool Stars 23 splinter session “Open Clusters as Laboratories for Cool Star Evolution”, held on 15 June 2026 in Tokyo, Japan. The session comprised one invited review, ten contributed talks, and ten poster pop-up presentations, organized around three themes: the evolution of rotation, magnetic activity, and chemical abundances (Li-depletion, [C/N], [Y/Mg], and neutron-capture elements). We close with a summary of the open questions identified in the panel discussion and the observational and theoretical work that new surveys (e.g. _Gaia_ DR4, 4MOST, WEAVE) and missions (e.g. PLATO, Roman) will enable over the coming years. Together, these efforts will help assess the current state of the field and shape its future directions.

## **ABSTRACT** 

_Context._ The recent discovery of filamentary stellar structures in the Milky Way disk raises the question of their formation in the context of the Galaxy evolution. 

_Aims._ In this work, we aim to kinematically and chemically characterize several filamentary stellar structures by looking for clues about their origin and formation mechanism. 

_Methods._ Recent works using machine-learning techniques and _Gaia_ data have identified many previously unknown Galactic strings. We cross-matched such data with the kinematics derived from the most recent _Gaia_ DR3 catalog as well as chemical data provided by the Galactic Archaeology with HERMES (GALAH) survey. 

_Results._ We found that most strings contain one or more open clusters and are kinematically hotter than open clusters (with internal velocity dispersions in the 1–7 km s[−][1] range) but cooler than field stars. 18 objects appear chemically homogeneous (σ[ _Fe_ / _H_ ] ≤ 0.1 dex), while two strings have a broad [Fe/H] distribution similar to the field stars but exhibit a different mean metallicity, which may identify them as migrating stellar structures. For seven objects the GALAH observations focus on the embedded open clusters; therefore, the chemical abundances are not representative of the whole structure. An object shows clues of chemical gradients along its extension in Galactic longitude. 

_Conclusions._ These objects may be evaporating or disrupted open clusters in which the chemical homogeneity is preserved in an unbound and expanding cloud of stars or co-moving stars belonging to a former and now disrupting star formation hub. In a few cases they appear to be moving groups with no chemical homogeneity, likely formed by the dynamical action of the Galactic bar or spiral arms. More data are needed to confirm such hypotheses. 

**Key words.** Galaxy: abundances – Galaxy: solar neighborhood – Stars: abundances – Open cluster and associations: general

## **1 Introduction** 

Galactic open clusters are groups of stars that formed from the same giant molecular cloud and therefore share approximately the same age, distance, and initial chemical composition. Their stars are loosely bound by mutual gravitational attraction, and while most open clusters survive for only a few hundred million years, the most massive systems can persist for several billion years ((VandenBerg & Stetson, 2004), with the most notable examples being M 67 and NGC 188). Because they contain stars spanning a wide range of masses but with broadly common ages and metallicities, 

open clusters provide natural laboratories for studying stellar evolution. 

Determining precise ages for cool stars remains one of the longstanding challenges in stellar astrophysics. This limitation also hinders our understanding of how key stellar properties, such as rotation, magnetic activity, and surface chemical abundances, evolve over time. Unlike fundamental properties such as effective temperature, radius, or composition, age cannot be measured directly for main-sequence stars. results.question: Compare the methods and main quantitative findings about cluster membership and substellar populations in the two studies: "EWOCS-IX: JWST/NIRCam observations of Westerlund 2 - Identification of candidate substellar members" and "The Comprehensive Investigations of the NGC 7419 Open Cluster and the New Perspective on Mass Populations". Specifically, (a) what membership or contamination-control approaches did each study use, and (b) what are the key quantitative results each reports about low-mass/substellar objects or mass populations (report numerical values stated in the papers)?
results.reference_answer:
a) Membership / contamination-control approaches:
- EWOCS-IX: Characterizes contamination by observing a nearby control field (CF) with identical filter coverage and observing strategy to enable statistical decontamination of the science field; performs PSF photometry with DOLPHOT and validates SED-fitting against synthetic JWST photometry of spectroscopically confirmed young brown dwarfs and simulated field contaminants to ensure robustness against reddened evolved stars (evidence: 4a5be3cb6eead38c3b4245e7; 87034cc1c6f388e66f9825f5).
- NGC 7419 study: Uses the HDBSCAN clustering algorithm within the pyUPMASK framework on five-dimensional Gaia DR3 astrometric space to assign kinematic membership probabilities, thereby separating cluster members from the dense Galactic background and isolating outliers as noise (evidence: 51314b7918ebd1b8131a89f2).

b) Key quantitative results about low-mass/substellar objects or mass populations:
- EWOCS-IX (Westerlund 2): The JWST/NIRCam dataset (10 wide/medium filters spanning 1.15–4.1 μm) reaches a 50% completeness limit at 0.015–0.02 M⊙ (~15–20 M_Jup) for the adopted distance (4.44 kpc), age (1–2 Myr), and A_V = 6.5 mag. Applying their validated SED-fitting methodology they identify 353 substellar candidates, of which 301 are classified as strong candidates and 52 as weak candidates. Comparison with the control field indicates the contamination level of the strong candidate sample is ≲5% down to masses of ~0.01–0.015 M⊙. They also identify 73 substellar candidates exhibiting infrared excess consistent with circumstellar disks; among those with reliable F410M photometry these represent 27.7(+3.4/−3.3)% of that subsample (evidence: 4a5be3cb6eead38c3b4245e7; 87034cc1c6f388e66f9825f5; 9b88ba4ffbfdd86c9401be27).
- NGC 7419 study: The membership pipeline was applied to 5,784 sources within 12′ of the cluster centre to derive kinematic membership probabilities. From orbital integrations (galpy) they report a high total peculiar spatial velocity V_LSR = 102.84 ± 3.00 km s−1 and, regarding mass distribution, they find that NGC 7419's mass distribution is best described by a three-component Gaussian model (i.e., three statistically distinct 'mass populations'), a result they quantify qualitatively and note was reproduced in another cluster (NGC 2168) (evidence: 51314b7918ebd1b8131a89f2; a8d5342f38ed3805a8102144; b4d37a99e7b52cc02d2e5470).

Summary comparison: EWOCS-IX relies on matched control-field observations plus photometric SED-fitting validation to statistically decontaminate and characterize a deep substellar census down to ~0.015 M⊙ with low contamination (~≤5%) among strong candidates, and reports a substantial disk-bearing fraction (~28%) among those with reliable mid-NIR photometry. The NGC 7419 study uses astrometric clustering (HDBSCAN in pyUPMASK) on Gaia DR3 to produce a high-purity membership catalogue for several thousand stars, reports unusual kinematics (V_LSR ≈ 102.8 km s−1) and a multicomponent (three-Gaussian) stellar mass distribution rather than focusing on substellar census (evidence: all cited).

## **5. Conclusions** 

We have presented deep JWST/NIRCam imaging of the supermassive young cluster Wd2, obtained as part of the EWOCS program. The presented dataset comprises 10 wide and mediumband filters spanning 1.15–4.1 µm, designed to enable a comprehensive analysis of the cluster. The JWST-enabled observations of BDs in distant clusters are not without new challenges. In this paper we use JWST/NIRCam to identify BDs in the young massive cluster Westerlund 2 (Wd2), using photometry in a wide range of filters across the 1.15-4.1 µ _m_ range. Wd2 is a ∼1-2 Myr-old, massive young cluster located at a distance of ∼4.4 kpc in the RCW 49 star-forming complex (Zeidler et al. 2015; Maíz Apellániz et al. 2022). It is among the most massive young clusters in the Milky Way, hosting numerous O-type stars and a total stellar cluster mass of ∼36,000 _M_ ⊙ (Zeidler et al. 2017). With a stellar mass well above 10[4] _M_ ⊙, Wd2 belongs to the class of so-called supermassive star clusters (Portegies Zwart et al. 2010). Its massive stellar content, high stellar density, and strong feedback environment make it an ideal laboratory for testing how extreme conditions influence the properties of substellar objects located at the bottom of the IMF. 

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the NIRCam observations and data reduction; Section 3 details the PSF photometric analysis and the extraction of a catalog in all filters; Section 4 presents the identification of substellar candidates via spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting; and Section 5 summarizes the results and conclusions.

## ABSTRACT 

Dense nuclear star clusters provide unique environments for studying the dynamical interactions between stars and massive black holes. When an accretion disk is present, dissipative star–disk interactions can capture surrounding stars, drive their inward migration, and ultimately lead to disk-induced tidal disruption events (dTDEs). The long-term feeding rate from this process, however, cannot be inferred from single-orbit migration estimates alone, as it depends on the coupled evolution of disk capture, collisional relaxation, stellar depletion and replenishment, and physical mergers within the star cluster. In this work, we use high-performance direct _N_ -body simulations combined with analytic prescriptions for star–disk interactions to follow this coupled evolution for intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) with accretion disks embedded in dense stellar clusters. The simulations track the formation of the stellar cusp, the capture of stars by repeated disk crossings, their subsequent orbital damping and migration, and their eventual consumption by the central IMBH. We find that dTDEs can sustain stellar mass supply rates of _∼_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] , which exceeds the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate for IMBHs with _M• <_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . These results identify dTDEs as an efficient stellar feeding channel for IMBHs in gas-rich dense stellar systems. As one possible application, this mechanism may help transform _∼_ 10[3] _M⊙_ IMBHs into more massive black-hole seeds, provided that compact stellar clusters and accretion disks persist for _>_ 30 Myr.

disk interactions can act as a dissipative conveyor of stellar material: the disk captures stars from a threedimensional cluster, damps their orbits, and delivers them inward on a migration timescale. 

This mechanism is especially relevant for intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). For _M•_ ≲ 10[5] _M⊙_ , the dTDE mass supply rate can exceed the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate, and may therefore dominate the early mass budget of the black hole. The problem is not simply whether an individual star can be captured by the disk; that can be estimated from local drag and migration timescales. The central question is whether a realistic collisional stellar cluster can maintain a continuous supply of stars to the disk after the innermost stars have been consumed. The answer depends on several coupled processes: the formation of a stellar cusp around the IMBH, two-body relaxation that refills the disk-crossing population, stochastic few-body encounters, mass segregation and stellar evolution, and physical collisions among stars that captured by the disk. These effects determine both the dTDE rate and the mass spectrum of the disrupted stars.

In summary, we confirm previous results that there is a hefty sequence of unresolved binaries in Trumpler 19 (Jadhav & Roy, 2021; Donada et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024; Sheikh et al., 2025). We also report the discovery of a sequence of unresolved triple and quadruple systems in this cluster, providing spectroscopic confirmation of some of the multiple systems. Within the uncertainties, the fraction of multiple stars in this cluster is comparable to that of the solar neighborhood, with the caveat that the local sample probes deeper down the main sequence. This fraction of unresolved triples and quadruples is also higher than that of the open cluster M 67, which has the same age and chemical composition. 

ple systems that lie above the binary sequence of equal-mass stars. The VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey allows us to close the loop, confirming membership for unresolved triple and quadruple systems in star clusters such as Trumpler 19. 

Unresolved triples and quadruples have been previously detected in some young open clusters and associations with ages of _t_ < 100 Myr (e.g., Gonzalez et al., 2014; Tokovinin, 2023; Malofeeva et al., 2023). However, the main result of this work is the proof that a population of triple and quadruple systems can manage to survive in an aged open cluster for a long time (over gigayears). This leads to many open questions that need to be answered: 

— How a large number of multiple systems affects the cluster evolution. This scenario was explored by Kiseleva et al. (1996) and Leigh & Geller (2013). 

— Why Trumpler 19 has more unresolved multiple systems than M 67, a cluster with a similar mass and age. 

— Whether this is a primordial feature, or the result of dynamical evolution (i.e., M 67 managed to destroy multiple systems more efficiently than Trumpler 19).

## **ABSTRACT** 

_Context._ It is difficult to identify unresolved triple and higher-order systems beyond the solar vicinity. Star clusters yield controlled environments with known physical parameters, providing a way to explore homogeneous stellar samples. 

_Aims._ Combining modern optical and near-IR surveys, our main goal is to explore the region of the color-magnitude diagrams located above the sequence of equal-mass binaries, which is inhabited by unresolved triple and quadruple systems. Specifically, here we aim to discover and characterize the presence of multiple systems in the aged open star cluster Trumpler 19. _Methods._ We selected cluster members using Gaia astrometry and photometry from the VVVX and DECAPS2 surveys. We made optical and near-IR color-magnitude diagrams to select stars located > 0.75 mag above the cluster main sequence, including suitable unresolved triple and quadruple systems. 

- _Results._ We confirm previous results that there is a sizable sequence of unresolved binaries in Trumpler 19. We also report the discovery of a sequence of unresolved multiple systems in this cluster, and confirm some of these multiple systems via radial velocities measured by the ESO KMOS VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey. The fraction of multiple stars in this cluster is comparable to that of the solar neighborhood, with the caveat that the local sample probes deeper down the main sequence. The fraction of unresolved triples and quadruples is also three times higher than that of the open cluster M 67, which is of a similar age and chemical composition. 

_Conclusions._ The discovery of unresolved triple systems in Trumpler 19 leads to our main conclusion that these systems were able to survive within the cluster for nearly 4 Gyr. In addition, this cluster contains more multiple systems than M 67, which has a similar total present mass. Further investigations are needed to unveil if this is a primordial feature or the result of dynamical evolution. 

**Key words.** Galaxy : disk – Galaxy: open clusters : general – Galaxy: open clusters: individual: Trumpler 19 – Infrared : stars – Surveys

We can cite a few specific examples such as M 67 (Sandquist et al., 2003), NGC2516 and NGC6530 (Gonzalez et al., 2014), NGC6819 (Brewer et al., 2016), and Ruprecht 147 (Torres et al., 2021). However, a sequence such as the one we observe here has never been reported. The comparison with the open cluster M 67 in particular is very interesting, because this cluster has a similar age ( _t_ = 4 Gyr), and metallicity ( _Z_ = 0), as Trumpler 19, and it is very well studied because it is located at _d_ = 900 pc, significantly closer than Trumpler 19, with _d_ = 2300 pc. The CMDs of M 67 (Leiner et al., 2025) show that there are a couple of stars in the region associated with triple and quadruple systems, but these do not form a sequence similar to the one we find in Trumpler 19. This indicates that the multiplicity fractions for these two clusters of a similar age are very different. We measure the unresolved triple and higher-order fraction as defined by Offner et al. (2023), finding that this fraction in Trumpler 19 (THF = 0.084 ± 0.010) is higher than that of the open cluster M 67 (THF = 0.029 ± 0.010). Therefore, there are nearly three times more unresolved triples and quadruples in Trumpler19 than in M 67. This fraction was measured within the color range 2.25 < _BP_ − _Ks_ < 4.75 mag for Trumpler 19, and 1.80 < _BP_ − _Ks_ < 4.30 mag for M 67, respectively (the color difference is due to the different mean cluster reddenings). This color range corresponds approximately to MS stars of spectral types roughly from G5V to M0V, temperatures from 3800 K to 5300 K, and masses within 0.5 < _M_ / _Mo_ < 0.9 (even though it is not straightforward to apply these parameters for our targets because they are composite systems).

results.question: Compare the explanations and formation mechanisms proposed in (1) "Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group" and (2) "The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots" for producing systems with unusual baryonic compositions. Specifically: (a) For the NGC 1052 paper, summarize the mechanism that produces dark-matter-deficient dwarfs and the key spatial/kinematic constraint it predicts (name the paper in your answer). (b) For the Little Red Dots paper, summarize the nucleosynthetic source it argues is required to produce strong Al enhancement with Mg depletion and the observational/analysis method used to infer these abundance patterns (name the paper in your answer). Finally (c) explicitly synthesize whether the nucleosynthetic requirements identified for Little Red Dots could be produced within tidal dwarf galaxies formed by the NGC 1052 major-merger scenario, citing supporting facts from both papers and stating any limitations noted in the excerpts.
results.reference_answer: (a) In "Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group," the authors argue that a major merger experienced by NGC 1052 produces tidal tails populated by tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs) that reproduce the intrinsic properties and alignment of the observed dark-matter–deficient dwarfs; the scenario predicts tidal tails elongated in many directions but limited to ~1 Mpc in length and implies specific spatial/kinematic configurations tied to the merger (radial orbits, near 1:1 mass ratio, specific progenitor orientations) (evidence: 1080978cacdd4f1923864231; 7970ef9bb839222221160264). (b) In "The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots," the authors conclude that the extreme aluminum enhancement coupled with strong magnesium depletion requires a source capable of exceptionally hot hydrogen burning with efficient mixing throughout a hydrogen-rich stellar core (motivating supermassive-star-like progenitors rather than only massive-star WR or AGB channels); they infer these abundance patterns from UV/absorption-line spectroscopy with ionization corrections anchored to observed Si II/Si IV ratios and decomposition of resonance-line P-Cygni profiles to measure column densities (evidence: 73c0dd94049421bf60675e32; 4b03a56505b3df90eced8c45). (c) Synthesis: The NGC 1052 paper demonstrates formation of DM-deficient TDGs via major-galaxy merger tidal tails (1080978cacdd4f1923864231), while the Little Red Dots paper requires internal high-temperature hydrogen-burning sources (supermassive-star-like) to produce the Al/Mg pattern (73c0dd94049421bf60675e32). The provided excerpts do not present evidence that TDGs formed in the NGC 1052 merger would host the specific progenitors (supermassive stars with the required hot H-burning and mixing) or the rapid internal chemical processing invoked for Little Red Dots. Therefore, based on the supplied excerpts, one cannot conclude TDGs from the NGC 1052 scenario would produce the observed Al-enhanced, Mg-depleted abundance patterns; the NGC 1052 paper also notes limitations in precise modelling and lacks stellar-nucleosynthesis details relevant to this question (evidence: 1080978cacdd4f1923864231; e1b987ad68b0187dfe898157).
results.answer:
In 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' the authors propose that the observed dark-matter-deficient dwarfs can be tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs) formed in long-lived tidal tails produced by a tuned head-on 1:1 major merger that generated the E4 morphology of NGC 1052. [1]

The same paper ('Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group') predicts that these DM-deficient dwarfs will be associated with the remnant galaxy and aligned along tidal tails (i.e., an alignment along a trail is a key spatial constraint). [1] [2]

The authors of 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' state that producing the E4 morphology and associated tidal tails requires radial orbits, a moderate gas fraction, a mass ratio close to 1:1, and specific progenitor orientations to remove most of the angular momentum. [2]

The abstract of 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' reports that the simulated tidal dwarf galaxies have sizes similar to the observed DM-deficient dwarfs but that the simulations cannot reproduce the luminous globular cluster systems because of resolution limitations. [1]

In 'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots' the authors report magnesium-depleted and aluminum-enhanced gas in Little Red Dots with a metallicity only ≈1% of the Sun, inferred using deep JWST spectroscopy from the SPURS program. [3]

The same paper ('The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots') interprets the Mg-depleted/Al-enhanced pattern as reproduced by hot hydrogen burning in fully convective supermassive stars, with the measured abundances implying stellar masses of at least 10,000 solar masses. [3]

'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots' constrains the nucleosynthetic burning temperature required to produce strong magnesium depletion and aluminum enhancement to approximately 73–81 MK. [4]

'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots' reports that comparable Al-rich/Mg-poor abundance patterns are not found in local comparison samples (e.g., the CLASSY UV sample), indicating the pattern is highly unusual outside globular clusters. [4]

Because 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' does not model detailed nucleosynthesis and explicitly states it cannot reproduce luminous globular cluster systems due to resolution limitations, that paper does not demonstrate that the supermassive-star, hot-hydrogen-burning conditions (≳70 MK in cores of ≥10,000 M⊙ stars) identified by 'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars...' would be produced within tidal dwarf galaxies formed in its major-merger scenario. [1] [3] [4]

'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' further notes limitations—specifically a very large simulation parameter space and insufficiently precise constraints on NGC 1052 and its dwarfs—that prevented more accurate reproduction of the observations, which limits the paper's ability to assess whether TDGs could reproduce exotic abundance patterns. [2]

## **1. Introduction** 

NGC1052-DF2 (Müller et al. 2019). Using numerical simulations, Bournaud & Duc (2006) showed that tidal satellites should be found more frequently around early-type galaxies. The formation of an elliptical galaxy has been modelled by, for example, Wang et al. (2020) to reproduce the properties of Cen A. Both Cen A and NGC 1052 have Seyfert 2 type active nuclei and massive black holes (Wang et al. 2020; Koss et al. 2022), whose formation and growth are likely related to mergers (Hopkins et al. 2006). 

The discovery of dark matter (DM) deficient dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group has attracted considerable attention and generated many debates over the past 8 years (van Dokkum et al. 2018, 2019). For example, Monelli & Trujillo (2019) argued that the mass based on dynamics of surrounding globular clusters (GCs) of NGC1052-DF2 could have been underestimated due to a distance overestimate. However, a more accurate distance based on the tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) stars has been obtained (Shen et al. 2021), confirming the distance of two DMdeficient dwarfs, DF2 and DF4, at ∼ 20 Mpc (see also Tang et al. 2026). 

In this paper we investigate whether the chain of DMdeficient dwarfs could be associated with a tidal tail, which would have been formed during a merger similar to that described by Wang et al. (2020). The goal is not to fully reproduce the observations of the NGC 1052 field but to verify whether this hypothesis may be compelling in comparison with the bullet dwarf model described by Lee et al. (2024) and by Keim et al. (2025). In Sect. 2 we describe the mechanism and associated parameters necessary to form an elliptical galaxy such as Cen A and NGC 1052. Section 3 shows how such a model may generate tidal tails and associated tidal dwarfs, and we also compare how realistically it may reproduce the observations. In Sect. 4 we compare and discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the two competitive models, the result of which is summarised in Section 5.

The observed combination of strong magnesium depletion, aluminum enhancement and little silicon enrichment therefore confines the burning temperature to approximately 73–81 MK. We illustrate the contrasting abundance patterns produced by alpha capture and hot hydrogen burning nucleosynthetic pathways in Figure 3. 

Such an Al-rich, Mg-poor signature is highly unusual outside GCs. Although anomalous light-element abundances – most commonly nitrogen enrichment – are widespread among GC stars and are also found in field populations thought to originate in now-disrupted clusters[35,36] , the extreme combination of magnesium depletion and aluminum enhancement observed here is much rarer. This pattern has so far been observed only in the oldest, most massive and most metal-poor GCs[37,38] , where it requires proton-capture burning at _T_ core ≳ 70 MK. No secure non-cluster analog of this extreme abundance pattern is known. We therefore searched for comparable aluminum enhancement in galaxies. 

We do not find a comparable abundance pattern in either extreme local star-forming galaxies or in ordinary galaxies matched to the LRDs in redshift and UV luminosity. At low redshift ( _z <_ 0 _._ 2), we compare to the COS Legacy Archive Spectroscopic SurveY[41] , a deep ultraviolet spectroscopic atlas of 45 galaxies spanning 6 _._ 2 _<_ log _M⋆_ ( _M⊙_ ) _<_ 10 _._ 1, with star-formation rates enhanced by _∼_ 2 dex over the _z ∼_ 0 starforming main sequence and therefore more representative of the intense star formation seen at _z >_ 2. **The relative abundances of elements in galaxies serve as fossil records of the physical conditions and processes by which they were forged. While the Big Bang produced only the lightest elements, subsequent stellar nucleosynthesis imprinted characteristic abundance patterns onto the surrounding gas, set initially by the temperatures reached inside stars and subsequently shaped by how the processed material was mixed and released. Globular clusters – dense, ancient groups of stars – provide a striking unique example. Some contain stars depleted in magnesium and enriched in aluminum, showing that they formed from gas exposed to exceptionally hot hydrogen burning. The stars responsible remain unknown. Little Red Dots[1] may provide this missing engine. These compact, luminous objects formed at cosmic epochs similar to those associated with globular-cluster formation[2,3] and are enshrouded by dense gas[4–7] whose chemical composition can be measured with the James Webb Space Telescope. Here, using deep spectroscopy from the SPURS program, we show that this abundance pattern characterizes the LRD central engine: magnesium-depleted and aluminum-enhanced gas with a metallicity only 1% that of the Sun. This pattern is not produced by ordinary massive stars at these redshifts and cannot be mimicked by ionization, gas geometry or dust. Instead, it is reproduced by hot hydrogen burning in fully convective supermassive stars, with the measured abundances implying masses of at least 10,000 solar masses – approximately 100 times larger than any star observed in the present-day Universe[8–10] . Little Red Dots may therefore reveal supermassive stars during their brief lives or in the immediate aftermath of their direct collapse, simultaneously identifying the long-sought source of globular cluster abundance anomalies and a formation pathway for massive black hole seeds.** 

Little red dots (LRDs)[1] have emerged as one of the most enigmatic populations discovered in the early Universe. Initially interpreted as extraordinarily compact galaxies (≲ 40 pc; unresolved in the rest-optical even with JWST[11] ) that had assembled implausibly large stellar masses within the first billion years after the Big Bang[12,13] , this picture was soon challenged by the first JWST spectra. These observations revealed that LRDs have 

nearly ubiquitous broad emission lines from rapidly moving gas, resembling those seen around actively growing supermassive black holes[1,11,14,15] .

## **5. Conclusions** 

In this work, we have verified that a major merger experienced by NGC 1052 produces tidal tails and TDGs that match the intrinsic properties of DM-deficient dwarfs discovered by van Dokkum et al. (2018, 2019) as well as their alignment along a trail. Our finding results from simple adaptations of the N- body hydrodynamical simulations made by Wang et al. (2020) to reproduce the properties of Cen A, and we addressed the supposed failures of the TDG scenario. The only limitation of our - modelling comes from its very large parameter space and insuffi ciently precise constraints on NGC 1052 and associated dwarfs, which prevented us from experimenting with a more accurate reproduction of the observations. 

According to the hierarchical scenario, the present-day E4 morphology of NGC 1052 takes its origin from its last major merger, which requires radial orbits, moderate gas fraction, a mass ratio close to 1:1, and specific orientations of the progenitor galaxies (Wang et al. 2020). The latter conditions are necessary to remove most of the angular momentum in the remnant, which is currently accompanied by large tidal tails and TDGs and match better the observations when compared to the bulletdwarf scenario. 

The bullet-dwarf scenario suffers from two major difficulties: first, reproducing the dwarf progenitors and, second, providing far too compact DM-deficient dwarfs. The scenario also neglects the fact that NGC 1052 is an active nucleus E4 galaxy showing tides, and it has likely experienced a major merger that can produce TDGs resembling the observed DM-deficient dwarfs. The likely occurrence of massive galaxy mergers near NGC 1052 has to be compared to the very rare dwarf–dwarf collision events in the field, for which only ten have been found in a (100Mpc)[3] volume from _z_ =3 to _z_ =0 (Lee et al. 2024). Future observations of dwarf radial distances will probe which of the two scenarios is the most likely. The dwarf GC over-luminosity appears to support the bullet-dwarf scenario, though there might be subtle selection effects associated with this property.

retrieved_chunks.text:
## **ABSTRACT** 

The discovery of dark matter-free (DM-free) dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 neighborhood has had a considerable impact on modern cosmology. The galaxies have been explained through a dwarf–dwarf head-on collision, a rare event. We find that they could alternatively be associated with a head-on 1:1 merger after it was tuned to generate the E4 morphology of NGC 1052. Our simulations show that such mergers produce long-lived tidal features, are associated with the remnant galaxy, and are in the form of large tidal tails, including tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs). We emphasise that such tidal features are predicted by the hierarchical scenario in which massive galaxies are formed by galaxy mergers. The latter can reproduce both the tidal features in the NGC1052 outskirts and the observed dwarf galaxies. The simulated TDGs have sizes similar to those observed, while they are ten times smaller in the bullet dwarf scenario. However, we cannot reproduce the luminous globular cluster systems due to resolution limitations. Resolving the radial distance between the DM-free dwarfs is necessary to identify the scenario of their formation. We suggest that there should be many other examples of DM-free dwarf galaxies in the neighbourhood of local massive galaxies and galaxy groups. 

**Key words.** Elliptical galaxies – dark matter – merger – dynamics

claims.text: In 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' the authors propose that the observed dark-matter-deficient dwarfs can be tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs) formed in long-lived tidal tails produced by a tuned head-on 1:1 major merger that generated the E4 morphology of NGC 1052.

The same paper ('Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group') predicts that these DM-deficient dwarfs will be associated with the remnant galaxy and aligned along tidal tails (i.e., an alignment along a trail is a key spatial constraint).

The authors of 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' state that producing the E4 morphology and associated tidal tails requires radial orbits, a moderate gas fraction, a mass ratio close to 1:1, and specific progenitor orientations to remove most of the angular momentum.

The abstract of 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' reports that the simulated tidal dwarf galaxies have sizes similar to the observed DM-deficient dwarfs but that the simulations cannot reproduce the luminous globular cluster systems because of resolution limitations.

In 'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots' the authors report magnesium-depleted and aluminum-enhanced gas in Little Red Dots with a metallicity only ≈1% of the Sun, inferred using deep JWST spectroscopy from the SPURS program.

The same paper ('The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots') interprets the Mg-depleted/Al-enhanced pattern as reproduced by hot hydrogen burning in fully convective supermassive stars, with the measured abundances implying stellar masses of at least 10,000 solar masses.

'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots' constrains the nucleosynthetic burning temperature required to produce strong magnesium depletion and aluminum enhancement to approximately 73–81 MK.

'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars: Globular Cluster-like Aluminum Enhancement in Little Red Dots' reports that comparable Al-rich/Mg-poor abundance patterns are not found in local comparison samples (e.g., the CLASSY UV sample), indicating the pattern is highly unusual outside globular clusters.

Because 'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' does not model detailed nucleosynthesis and explicitly states it cannot reproduce luminous globular cluster systems due to resolution limitations, that paper does not demonstrate that the supermassive-star, hot-hydrogen-burning conditions (≳70 MK in cores of ≥10,000 M⊙ stars) identified by 'The Ashes of Supermassive Stars...' would be produced within tidal dwarf galaxies formed in its major-merger scenario.

'Tidal origin of dark-matter free dwarf galaxies in the NGC 1052 group' further notes limitations—specifically a very large simulation parameter space and insufficiently precise constraints on NGC 1052 and its dwarfs—that prevented more accurate reproduction of the observations, which limits the paper's ability to assess whether TDGs could reproduce exotic abundance patterns.

results.question: Compare the evidence and proposed observational follow-ups in (1) "The youngest white dwarf companion to a millisecond pulsar: Insights from NGC 362D" and (2) "Planetary Nebula Central Stars as Tracers of Planetary Nebula–Star Cluster Associations in the Galaxy" regarding the role of spectroscopy for constraining companion/central-star properties. Specifically: which concrete spectral diagnostics does paper (1) propose to search for to test the residual circumstellar-material scenario for COM-NGC362D, and what broader spectroscopic needs and limitations does paper (2) identify for improving central-star (CS) parameter estimates? Provide an explicit synthesis that draws on both papers' recommendations.
results.reference_answer:
Paper (1) "The youngest white dwarf companion to a millisecond pulsar: Insights from NGC 362D" proposes concrete spectroscopic diagnostics: detection of narrow metal lines (explicitly motivated by detections in PSR J1816+4510) such as He I, Ca II, Si II, and Mg II, and measurement of the companion radial-velocity curve to constrain the binary mass ratio (evidence: e16574046febb2cf0a447e2d; d2c9f58109af70350b291b7c). Paper (1) links these metal-line detections to the presence of a lower-pressure environment associated with an expelled cloud of circumstellar material and suggests such lines would support the residual-material interpretative scenario (evidence: d2c9f58109af70350b291b7c).

Paper (2) "Planetary Nebula Central Stars as Tracers of Planetary Nebula–Star Cluster Associations in the Galaxy" identifies broader spectroscopic needs and limitations: it stresses the lack of adequate data for precise CS effective-temperature estimates as a major limitation for assessing candidate CS–cluster associations, and recommends deep spectroscopic nebular data and photoionization modelling to derive more precise CS physical properties (evidence: 043cf2bd326941e493456f18). It also notes that uncertainties in CS temperatures and luminosities (and assumptions made when temperatures are unavailable) limit evolutionary consistency checks (evidence: 20b09817ecfa63e067864be0).

Synthesis: Both papers converge on spectroscopy as a critical next step but at different, complementary levels. The MSP-WD study (paper 1) calls for high-resolution optical spectroscopy of the companion to (a) measure radial velocities (dynamical masses) and (b) detect narrow metal absorption lines (He I, Ca II, Si II, Mg II) that would be direct diagnostics of low-pressure expelled circumstellar material. The PN–cluster study (paper 2) emphasizes the need for deep nebular and stellar spectroscopy plus photoionization modelling to improve CS effective-temperature and luminosity estimates, which are necessary to test evolutionary consistency with cluster ages and the initial–final mass relation. Together, these recommendations imply a coordinated observational approach: for compact binary companions like COM-NGC362D, targeted high-resolution stellar spectroscopy to detect metal lines and radial-velocity variations; for CSs in cluster searches, deep nebular spectra and modelling to infer CS Teff and L. Implementing both types of spectroscopic programs would provide the direct compositional/dynamical diagnostics (paper 1) and the improved physical parameter estimates (paper 2) that are each required to robustly interpret post–mass-transfer objects and to confirm associations with clusters (evidence: e16574046febb2cf0a447e2d; d2c9f58109af70350b291b7c; 043cf2bd326941e493456f18; 20b09817ecfa63e067864be0).

We can thus argue that residual circumstellar material may persist around the companion star for a significant fraction of the pre-cooling timescale, potentially producing observable signatures at radio and optical wavelengths that are not predicted by standard evolutionary models and that can ultimately lead to the ambiguous or incorrect classification of such systems. 

Within this interpretative framework, the absence of radio eclipses in NGC362D (Ridolfi et al. in prep.) may be explained by the inhomogeneous and clumpy distribution of the surrounding material, as observed by Polzin et al. (2020) and Shang et al. (2024) for PSR J1816+4510 from the detection of dispersion measure fluctuations on short spatial and temporal scales. Alternatively, the expelled material may have a column density below the threshold required to produce detectable radio absorption or scattering at the observed frequencies. Finally, we also note that the optical companion to the MSP M2C (Li et al. 2025) appears to be very similar to COM-NGC362D. In fact, it is a young HeWD, at about 10 Myr since the beginning of its cooling, possibly showing a similar wavelength-dependent colour variation; this may suggest that it has been caught in the same transitional post-mass-transfer phase as COM-NGC362D. 

Given the brightness of COM-NGC362D, future spectroscopic observations could be used to measure the radial-velocity 

curve of the companion star, thereby placing strong constraints on the binary mass ratio. Moreover, the detection of narrow metal lines with profiles similar to those observed in PSR J1816+4510 (Kaplan et al. 2013) or by Leanza et al. (2025) for the case of UV-dim stars, would provide further support for the interpretative scenario we describe in this letter.

retrieved_chunks.text:
## **ABSTRACT** 

We report on the identification of the optical counterpart to the recently discovered millisecond pulsar (MSP) NGC362D in the Galactic globular cluster NGC 362 based on deep, multi-band, and multi-epoch _Hubble_ Space Telescope observations. Our analysis robustly shows that this object is a very low-mass (∼ 0.18 M⊙) He white dwarf (WD) still in the pre-cooling phase. Interestingly, a detailed comparison with updated binary evolution models indicates that this object completed the mass-transfer phase only recently (∼ 0.6 Gyr ago), thus strongly suggesting that COM-NGC362D is the youngest WD companion to a MSP identified to date. Remarkably, in this respect, the photometric properties of NGC362D show, for the first time in this class of objects, significant wavelength-dependent variations that are consistent with the presence of residual circumstellar material. This system therefore provides a valuable test case to directly probe the immediate aftermath of the MSP recycling process and to constrain the early evolutionary stages of proto-WD companions and their radio and optical properties. Our results suggest that residual material can produce radio and optical signatures that mimic those of systems with non-degenerate companions, potentially leading to the misclassification of young MSPs. 

**Key words.** globular clusters: individual (NGC 362) – pulsars: general – stars: evolution – binaries: general

## ABSTRACT 

Planetary nebulae (PNe) that are physically associated with star clusters are rare but crucial for stellar evolution studies because they allow their initial and final stellar properties to be determined independently, contributing to constraints on the initial-to-final-mass relation (IFMR), which traces stellar mass loss. Although the identification of such pairs is essential, most reported cases have been identified incidentally rather than through systematic searches. Here, we attempt to uncover new such associations in our Galaxy employing literature PN central stars (CSs) and star cluster catalogues. Exploring relevant angular positions on the sky and kinematic Gaia DR3 data, we identify 38 candidate CS-cluster pairs. The components of eight of these pairs present consistent interstellar extinctions, and their CS properties are compatible with stellar evolution models. Two of these candidate pairs are already reported in the literature as true associations. We evaluate separately the remaining six pairs using literature PN observational data, assessing the likelihood of each pair being a true association. The initial and final masses of our best candidates are mostly consistent with the latest IFMR predictions and confirmed cluster-PNe points. An additional 46 CS-cluster pairs have components with compatible angular positions but lack kinematic CS data and are thus presented separately. More data are needed for a precise estimation of the physical parameters of most of our candidates and to confirm these associations, which will be addressed in future studies. 

_Keywords:_ Planetary nebulae (1249) — Planetary nebulae nuclei (1250) — Star clusters (1567) — Catalogs (205) — Stellar astronomy (1583)

results.question: Compare the concrete emission-line kinematic findings reported in "SPURS: An Ultra-deep View Inside the Compact, Nitrogen-Enriched Nuclei of Little Red Dots" with the dynamical constraint on the Galactic bar's pattern speed reported in "Bar-induced migration of ω Centauri away from Gaia Sausage-Enceladus". Specifically: (a) What are the reported FWHM ranges for broad [O III] components across the Little Red Dots, and the best-fit broad N IV] FWHM for GN-2, as given in SPURS? (b) What minimum bar pattern speed (Ω_b,min) does Dillamore et al. report is required for the retrograde 1:1 resonance to migrate objects from the GSE debris to ω Cen's current orbit? (c) Based only on the cited values from these two papers, is the required Ω_b,min within, below, or above the typical recent estimates of the bar pattern speed cited by Dillamore et al. (give the comparison using the numeric ranges provided)?
results.reference_answer: (a) SPURS reports broad [O III] components with FWHM = 1130–1627 km s⁻¹ across the four LRDs, and a best-fit broad N IV] component in GN-2 with FWHM = 1514 ± 137 km s⁻¹ (evidence: 07507c678ea7f30347e2e8bd; af6b3a52a30546f12aac4336). (b) Dillamore et al. report that the retrograde 1:1 resonance can cause the migration only if the minimum bar pattern speed throughout its evolution was Ω_b,min ≲ 26 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ (evidence: dfb7f5ab73b1b616d9550fde). **Summary.** We have investigated the scenario in which the globular cluster _𝜔_ Cen originated in the GSE merger event (e.g. as a nuclear star cluster), and subsequently migrated to its current orbit due to resonance with the Galactic bar Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

Extending the chemical analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026), we find that the proposed metal-poor corridor between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen is not a chemically simple continuation of the main low- _𝛼_ GSE sequence. The low- _𝛼_ component is clearest near the GSE cloud and only tentatively reaches _𝜔_ Cen in the bridge slice that contains the cluster; elsewhere the bridge region is more _𝛼_ -enhanced than the GSE core. The chemical evidence therefore remains suggestive rather than conclusive: it is compatible with a GSE origin for _𝜔_ Cen, but does not require one. 

The retrograde 1:1 resonance is capable of causing migration of stars from the GSE debris to the current orbit of _𝜔_ Cen. This requires that the minimum pattern speed of the bar throughout its evolution was Ωb _,_ min ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This is considerably slower than most estimates of the current value (typically Ωb = 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] ), though consistent with Horta et al. (2025). 

In summary, the GSE/ _𝜔_ Cen migration scenario is plausible, but would require a re-evaluation of the general consensus on the bar’s pattern speed.

However, it has become clear in recent years that the Galactic bar causes significant perturbations to orbits in the inner stellar halo (Dillamore et al. 2023, 2024b, 2025; Dillamore & Sanders 2025; Tomlinson et al. 2026; De Leo et al. 2026; Gherghinescu et al. 2026). The bar’s pattern speed Ωb (rotation rate) is likely to be decelerating (Chiba et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2025), a process which can cause migration of globular clusters via resonances (Dillamore et al. 2024b). These include the retrograde 1:1 resonance, where the orbital frequencies of a particle satisfy Ω _𝜙_ − Ωb + Ω _𝑟_ = 0. Tomlinson et al. (2026) showed that this resonance can cause significant scattering of orbits along its length in ( _𝐿 𝑧, 𝐸_ ) space (on lines of gradient d _𝐸_ /d _𝐿 𝑧_ = Ωb; see Dillamore & Sanders 2025). This process could be responsible for deflecting _𝜔_ Cen onto lower energy, more retrograde orbits (Laporte & Orkney 2026). In this _Letter_ we investigate this scenario by running simulations in a realistic Milky Way potential with a decelerating bar. We determine the range of pattern speeds compatible with the migration of _𝜔_ Cen from the GSE debris, and thus assess how plausible this scenario is. We also analyse the chemical composition of retrograde substructure between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen, extending the analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

The rest of this _Letter_ is arranged as follows. In Section 2 we describe the data used, and analyse the chemistry of retrograde substructure. Section 3 discusses our simulations and the constraint on Ωb. Finally we discuss and summarise our conclusions in Section 4.

## ABSTRACT 

Large spectroscopic surveys require robust pipelines capable of inferring stellar parameters over a wide range of the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram from data of varying quality. SDSS-V is one such survey, where the data from the lower-resolution, optical BOSS spectrograph will provide a large dataset covering a wide range of Galactic stellar populations. To better analyze these data, we present BOSS-CLAM, a generative, forward modeling pipeline for inferring effective temperature ( _T_ eff ), surface gravity (log _g_ ), metallicity ([Fe _/_ H]), and _α−_ abundance ([ _α/_ M]) from continuum-normalized BOSS spectra. BOSS-CLAM maps stellar labels to Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) basis vector weights via a polynomial mapping jointly optimized with the spectral decomposition, which provides a more flexible framework for working with the lower-resolution BOSS data. Additionally, training labels are drawn from four complementary sources (ASPCAP, `BOSS-MINESweeper` , wide binaries, and a hot star validation sample), which enables coverage from cool M dwarfs through hot OB stars, and across a wide range of metallicity. We infer parameters for 1,708,214 BOSS spectra, with a recommended clean catalog of 915,514 sources. Validation against open and globular clusters demonstrates homogeneous, accurate abundances across a wide range of metallicity. Wide binary tests yield abundance uncertainties of _σ_ [Fe _/_ H] _≈_ 0 _._ 15 dex and _σ_ [ _α/_ M] _≈_ 0 _._ 06 dex at SNR = 10. retrieved_chunks.text: There are several methods that employ forward modeling of stellar spectra. The Cannon (M. Ness et al. 2015; A. R. Casey et al. 2016) predicts continuum-normalized spectra at fixed wavelengths from a set of reference labels. This method has been quite successful in inferring parameters from APOGEE spectra in SDSS-IV and SDSS-V ( Abdurro’uf et al. 2022; A. Behmard et al. 2025). The Cannon relies on two core assumptions: first, that spectra with identical stellar labels occupy a consistent low-dimensional manifold after continuum normalization, and second, that the training labels are both precise and representative of the underlying stellar population. Such assumptions are difficult to satisfy with the BOSS data. First, BOSS spectra can exhibit flux calibration issues (I. Medan et al. 2025) that can be minimized with careful normalization (I. Medan et al. 2025; A. R. Casey et al. 2026), but not completely removed. Second, constructing a homogeneous training set with precise labels across the full range of stellar populations observed by BOSS is challenging, particularly given the broad coverage of the HR diagram. Currently, the only pipeline that fits the above criteria is BOSSNet (L. Sizemore et al. 2024). BOSSNet is a data-driven discriminative model that utilizes a neural network to predict _T_ eff , log _g_ , and [Fe _/_ H] from BOSS spectra. For training, it drew labels from a variety of sources in order to cover a significant range of the HR diagram. On average, BOSSNet achieves these goals with high precision. However, there are some issues with these results. Primarily, there are significant systematic errors across the HR diagram. The top row of Figure 1 shows the difference between the stellar pa- 

rameters used for training in this work (True; Section 2) and the BOSSNet parameters. Significant biases are observed, especially for the subgiants and at the most metal-poor end. Additionally, as the model is discriminative, it tends to bias poorly-fitted parameters to the mean of the training distribution. Because of these issues, the goal of this paper is to develop a model that reduces systematic errors and avoids some of the pitfalls of discriminative models. 

In this work we focus on generative, forward-modeling approaches where stellar spectra are estimated from labels. Particularly when training a model with higherprecision labels relative to the spectra themselves, as is the case here, this has significant advantages. As discussed in Y.-S. Ting (2025), when the input features (in this case, lower resolution spectra) have much higher noise than the outputs (stellar labels from higher resolution spectra), this inevitably leads to attenuation bias in discriminative models. In a generative model, as the noisier spectrum is the dependent variable, only the variance of the model estimate is affected, not the bias. Additionally, during inference the uncertainty in the spectra is explicitly incorporated into the likelihood.

## 8. SUMMARY AND FUTURE WORK 

In this work, we develop a generative model to infer _T_ eff , log _g_ , [Fe _/_ H], [ _α/_ M] from SDSS-V BOSS spectra in DR20. The aim was to develop a model that covered a wide range of the HR diagram, improved on other pipelines used in SDSS-V, and was well-suited for the lower-resolution BOSS dataset. To accomplish this, we developed BOSS-CLAM. BOSS-CLAM forward models spectra by mapper stellar labels to NMF basis vector weights, which are combined with NMF basis vectors to represent BOSS spectra. This mapping and these basis vectors are optimized using a training set consisting of labels from ASPCAP, `MINESweeper` , wide binaries, and a hot star validation sample. The trained model is able to infer parameters from a wide range of parameter spaces with a high level of accuracy and precision.

Additionally, generative models that use synthetic spectra, such as the Payne (Y.-S. Ting et al. 2019), are not suited for these data. The Payne uses neural network interpolation of synthetic spectral grids to infer stellar labels, achieving high precision in APOGEE data. Such methods are sensitive to differences between the observed and synthetic spectra. These differences become increasingly important at lower resolutions, where broad spectral features and continuum variations can dominate the fit. Additionally, it is difficult to cover a wide range of the HR diagram with synthetic models, as many grids are known to produce incompatible spectra for e.g., low-mass stars (H. R. A. Jones et al. 2005; T. A. ten Brummelaar et al. 2005). 

In this work, we will outline the creation and training of a generative model, which we call the “BOSSCLAM”. BOSS-CLAM predicts continuum normalized spectra from stellar labels by optimizing a smooth, polynomial mapping between stellar parameters and Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF; D. Lee & H. S. Seung 2000) weights. These weights are multiplied by a series of NMF basis vectors to predict stellar spectra. Using a generative model avoids attenuation bias, the decomposition of the spectra with NMF helps remedy continuum normalization issues remaining in some of the data, and the choice of training data outlined will allow for predictions across the HR diagram, even when there are only partial training labels. 

The structure of this paper is as follows: Section 2 describes the training data used, Section 3 describes the BOSS-CLAM model, Section 4 outlines the stellar parameters inferred with BOSS-CLAM with the SDSS-V DR20 spectra, Section 5 demonstrates validation tests of the BOSS-CLAM parameters with data from external sources, Section 6 discusses some possible improvements 

that could be made to the method, Section 7 provides some examples of applications of these BOSS-CLAM parameters, and Section 8 provides a summary and some conclusions for this work.
